title: Cholesterol Calculator: Total/LDL/HDL Levels (ACC/AHA 2018) | Hacé Cuentas
description: Cholesterol calculator using ACC/AHA 2018 guidelines: check Total (<200), LDL (<100), HDL (>40 men / >50 women), and non-HDL targets. Clinician-grade interpretation.
intro:
A standard lipid panel reports five numbers — total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, and non-HDL cholesterol — and each one carries a different weight in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk stratification. This calculator applies the cutoffs adopted in the 2018 ACC/AHA Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guideline (Grundy et al., Circulation 2019), which superseded the older NCEP ATP III framework from 2001. The shift matters: ATP III emphasized rigid LDL targets, while the 2018 guideline embeds those numbers inside a 10-year ASCVD risk estimate (Pooled Cohort Equations) and a shared-decision conversation between patient and clinician.

The operative thresholds in mg/dL are well established. Total cholesterol is desirable below 200, borderline 200–239, and high at 240 or above. LDL is optimal below 100, near-optimal 100–129, borderline 130–159, high 160–189, and very high at 190 or above — the last category triggers statin therapy regardless of 10-year risk score because it raises suspicion for familial hypercholesterolemia. HDL is protective above 40 mg/dL in men and above 50 mg/dL in women; below those values it counts as an ASCVD risk enhancer. Triglycerides are normal below 150, borderline 150–199, high 200–499, and very high at 500 or above (pancreatitis risk).

Non-HDL cholesterol (Total minus HDL) deserves explicit attention. Multiple meta-analyses, including the seminal JAMA 2012 paper by Boekholdt et al., showed non-HDL outperforms LDL-C as a predictor of cardiovascular events, especially when triglycerides are elevated. The non-HDL target is simply LDL target + 30, so optimal is below 130 mg/dL.

The results below should be interpreted alongside your ASCVD 10-year risk score (free at tools.acc.org/ascvd-risk-estimator-plus). A 55-year-old patient with LDL 145 mg/dL and 10-year risk under 5% may need only lifestyle intervention; the same LDL with risk above 7.5% pushes the conversation toward moderate-intensity statin therapy. Educational tool only — not a substitute for an in-person evaluation with your primary care physician or cardiologist.
keyTakeaway: ACC/AHA 2018 targets (mg/dL): Total <200, LDL <100 optimal / ≥190 statin-mandatory, HDL >40 men / >50 women, Triglycerides <150, non-HDL <130. LDL ≥190 or 10-yr ASCVD risk ≥7.5% generally indicates statin therapy.

useCases.title: Post-physical lipid panel interpretation
useCases.description: A 48-year-old male executive picks up his annual physical results: Total 232 mg/dL, LDL 152 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL, Triglycerides 188 mg/dL. The calculator flags Total as borderline-high, LDL as borderline-high, HDL below the male protective threshold (40), and triglycerides borderline. Non-HDL works out to 194 mg/dL — well above the 130 target. He brings this breakdown to his PCP, who runs the ASCVD risk calculator (10-year risk 9.2%) and recommends initiating moderate-intensity rosuvastatin 10 mg per ACC/AHA 2018 Class IIa indication.

useCases.title: Statin eligibility screening (primary prevention)
useCases.description: A 56-year-old woman with hypertension on lisinopril and a 30-pack-year smoking history has Total 218, LDL 142, HDL 48, Trig 162. The calculator confirms LDL is borderline-high and HDL is below the female 50 mg/dL threshold. Her ASCVD 10-year risk computes to 12.4%, placing her in the intermediate-to-high category. Per the 2018 guideline, this triggers a clinician-patient risk discussion, and she elects to start atorvastatin 20 mg with goal of LDL reduction ≥30% (moderate intensity) or ≥50% (high intensity).

useCases.title: Family history / FH genetic screening
useCases.description: A 32-year-old man whose father had a myocardial infarction at age 44 gets a lipid panel: Total 298, LDL 218, HDL 52, Trig 140. The calculator flags LDL as very-high (≥190), which per ACC/AHA 2018 mandates statin therapy regardless of 10-year ASCVD risk and raises strong suspicion for heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH). He is referred to a lipid specialist for genetic testing (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9 mutations) and cascade screening of first-degree relatives. High-intensity rosuvastatin 40 mg is initiated.

useCases.title: Lifestyle intervention response monitoring
useCases.description: A 58-year-old with metabolic syndrome adopted a Mediterranean-style diet, added 30 g/day soluble fiber, and started 200 minutes/week of moderate aerobic exercise. Baseline: Total 244, LDL 158, HDL 41, Trig 210. After 16 weeks: Total 198, LDL 118, HDL 49, Trig 138. The calculator shows Total and triglycerides now in optimal range, LDL improved from borderline-high to near-optimal, and HDL gained 8 mg/dL — consistent with the expected 10–20% LDL reduction from intensive lifestyle change. Statin discussion is deferred for another 12 weeks of monitoring.

useCases.title: Diabetic patient lipid target check
useCases.description: A 62-year-old type 2 diabetic on metformin has Total 196, LDL 112, HDL 44, Trig 178. Per ACC/AHA 2018, all diabetic adults aged 40–75 with LDL 70–189 mg/dL warrant at least moderate-intensity statin therapy regardless of 10-year risk. The calculator confirms LDL is near-optimal but above the diabetes-specific aggressive target of <70 mg/dL recommended for high-risk diabetics. Atorvastatin 40 mg is added with goal of ≥50% LDL reduction.

useCases.title: Severe hypertriglyceridemia pancreatitis risk
useCases.description: A 44-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes and central obesity reports vague abdominal discomfort. Lipid panel: Total 312, HDL 28, Trig 612. Calculator flags HDL critically low and triglycerides in the very-high category (≥500), which carries acute pancreatitis risk. The Friedewald LDL calculation is invalid above Trig 400, so direct LDL or Martin-Hopkins estimation is required. Immediate referral for fenofibrate or omega-3 (icosapent ethyl 2 g BID per REDUCE-IT) plus glycemic optimization. ER threshold: Trig >1000 or pancreatitis symptoms.

useCases.title: Post-MI secondary prevention check
useCases.description: A 67-year-old man six months out from anterior STEMI is on high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg. Latest panel: Total 142, LDL 64, HDL 46, Trig 158. The calculator confirms LDL well below the secondary-prevention target of <70 mg/dL (some guidelines now suggest <55 mg/dL post-event per 2018 ACC/AHA and 2019 ESC consensus). Treatment is working as intended. If LDL remained ≥70 despite max statin, ezetimibe 10 mg or a PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab, evolocumab) would be considered.

useCases.title: Young adult Lp(a) and FH screening trigger
useCases.description: A 28-year-old endurance athlete with no traditional risk factors has Total 252, LDL 178, HDL 68, Trig 78. The calculator flags LDL as high, but HDL is excellent and trigs are great. Given the elevated LDL despite athletic lifestyle and lean body composition, the clinician adds an Lp(a) assay (elevated in 20% of population, independent ASCVD risk factor) and considers genetic FH testing. ACC/AHA 2018 recommends Lp(a) measurement once in adulthood, especially with personal or family history of premature ASCVD.

explanation:
## Lipid Panel Components and ACC/AHA 2018 Cutoffs

The 2018 ACC/AHA Cholesterol Clinical Practice Guideline (Grundy et al., Circulation 2019; 139:e1082-e1143) reorganized adult cholesterol management around three principles: estimate 10-year ASCVD risk with the Pooled Cohort Equations, identify risk enhancers, and have a clinician-patient risk discussion before initiating statin therapy. The threshold values used in this calculator align directly with that framework.

**Total cholesterol (mg/dL):** Desirable <200, borderline-high 200-239, high ≥240. Total alone is a coarse marker; its main utility is as a screening trigger.

**LDL cholesterol (mg/dL):** Optimal <100, near-optimal 100-129, borderline-high 130-159, high 160-189, very high ≥190. LDL ≥190 is a hard statin indication regardless of risk score because it strongly suggests genetic hypercholesterolemia.

**HDL cholesterol (mg/dL):** Protective threshold is >40 in men and >50 in women. Below those values it counts as an ASCVD risk-enhancing factor. HDL above 60 was historically considered a 'negative risk factor' but recent Mendelian randomization data (including HPS3/TIMI55-REVEAL) suggest extremely high HDL (>100) may not provide additional benefit.

**Triglycerides (mg/dL):** Normal <150, borderline 150-199, high 200-499, very high ≥500. Levels ≥500 carry acute pancreatitis risk and warrant fibrate or icosapent ethyl therapy.

## How LDL Is Calculated — Friedewald and Its Limits

Most standard lipid panels do not measure LDL directly. Instead they estimate it using the Friedewald equation (Friedewald, Levy, Fredrickson; Clin Chem 1972):

**LDL = Total Cholesterol − HDL − (Triglycerides ÷ 5)**

This works reliably when triglycerides are below 400 mg/dL. Above that, the equation systematically underestimates LDL because the Trig/5 approximation of VLDL cholesterol breaks down. Two alternatives are used in modern labs:

- **Martin-Hopkins equation** (Martin et al., JAMA 2013): uses an adjustable divisor based on triglyceride and non-HDL strata. Accurate up to Trig ~800 mg/dL and the default in most major US health systems since ~2018.
- **Direct LDL assay**: enzymatic or immunoassay measurement, more expensive but mandatory at Trig >400.

When you see a 'calculated LDL' on your lab report and your triglycerides are high, ask whether direct LDL was used.

## Non-HDL Cholesterol — Often Better Than LDL

Non-HDL cholesterol = Total Cholesterol − HDL. It captures every atherogenic particle in one number: LDL, VLDL, IDL, chylomicron remnants, and Lp(a). Boekholdt et al. (JAMA 2012; 307:1302-1309) meta-analyzed 62,154 statin-treated patients and showed non-HDL outperformed LDL-C as a predictor of cardiovascular events. The non-HDL target is straightforward: LDL goal + 30. So optimal non-HDL is <130 mg/dL.

## ApoB — The Emerging Gold Standard

Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) counts atherogenic particles directly: one ApoB molecule per LDL, VLDL, IDL, and Lp(a) particle. Sniderman et al. (JACC 2019; 73:2150-2161) made the formal case that ApoB is causal in atherosclerosis and superior to both LDL-C and non-HDL for risk discrimination, especially in patients with metabolic syndrome, diabetes, or discordance between LDL-C and triglycerides. The 2018 ACC/AHA guideline lists ApoB ≥130 mg/dL as a risk-enhancing factor. The Canadian Cardiovascular Society (2021) and several European guidelines now place ApoB as a preferred target where available.

## Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH) Screening

Heterozygous FH affects approximately 1 in 250 people globally — making it more common than type 1 diabetes — but only 10% are diagnosed. Suspect FH when LDL is ≥190 mg/dL in adults (≥160 in children) without secondary causes, especially with personal or family history of premature ASCVD (men <55, women <65). Genetic testing covers LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9. Cascade screening of first-degree relatives is recommended. Untreated HeFH patients have a ~50% risk of coronary heart disease in men by age 50 and in women by age 60.

## Statin Indications (ACC/AHA 2018)

Four groups benefit clearly from statin therapy:

1. **Clinical ASCVD** (prior MI, stroke, PAD, revascularization) — high-intensity statin.
2. **LDL ≥190 mg/dL** — high-intensity statin regardless of risk score.
3. **Diabetes age 40-75 with LDL 70-189** — moderate-intensity statin minimum; high-intensity if 10-year ASCVD risk ≥20% or multiple risk enhancers.
4. **Primary prevention age 40-75 with LDL 70-189**: 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5% triggers a risk discussion; ≥20% supports high-intensity statin without need for additional risk stratification.

For borderline-risk patients (5-7.5%), coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring can refine the decision — a CAC of 0 in this group generally allows deferral of statin therapy.

## Evidence-Based Lifestyle Interventions

- **Mediterranean diet** (PREDIMED trial, NEJM 2018) — reduces major cardiovascular events ~30%. Emphasizes olive oil, nuts, fish, vegetables, legumes, whole grains.
- **Portfolio Diet** (Jenkins, JAMA 2003): plant sterols 2 g/day + soluble fiber 25-30 g/day + soy protein + nuts. Can reduce LDL by 13-30% — comparable to a low-intensity statin.
- **Soluble fiber** (oats, beans, psyllium): 5-10 g/day reduces LDL ~5%.
- **Plant stanols/sterols**: 2 g/day reduces LDL 6-10%.
- **Aerobic exercise**: 150-300 minutes/week moderate intensity, raises HDL 3-6 mg/dL and lowers triglycerides 10-20%.
- **Weight loss**: each 1 kg loss reduces LDL ~0.8 mg/dL and raises HDL ~0.35 mg/dL.

Lifestyle alone rarely lowers LDL more than 20-30%; for LDL ≥190 or established ASCVD, lifestyle is adjunct to pharmacotherapy, not a replacement.

faq.q: What's a good LDL cholesterol level?
faq.a: Per the 2018 ACC/AHA Cholesterol Guideline, optimal LDL is below 100 mg/dL for primary prevention. Near-optimal is 100-129, borderline-high 130-159, high 160-189, and very high at 190 or above. For patients with established ASCVD (prior heart attack, stroke, revascularization, or PAD), the target tightens to below 70 mg/dL, and recent 2022 ACC consensus and 2019 ESC guidelines push toward below 55 mg/dL after a recent event. For diabetics aged 40-75, moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended for LDL 70-189 even at lower risk scores. Any LDL ≥190 mg/dL is itself a statin indication regardless of 10-year ASCVD risk and should trigger evaluation for familial hypercholesterolemia.

faq.q: Why is HDL above 60 mg/dL considered protective?
faq.a: HDL particles perform reverse cholesterol transport: they accept free cholesterol from peripheral tissues including arterial macrophages, esterify it via LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase), and deliver it to the liver for excretion as bile acids. Higher HDL was historically associated with lower cardiovascular events in observational cohorts (Framingham, ARIC), leading to the 'negative risk factor' designation when HDL ≥60 mg/dL. However, Mendelian randomization studies and trials of HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors like torcetrapib and evacetrapib, niacin) have failed to show that raising HDL pharmacologically reduces cardiovascular events. The current view is that HDL functionality (cholesterol efflux capacity) matters more than absolute level, and very high HDL above ~90-100 mg/dL may not confer additional benefit and could occasionally reflect dysfunctional HDL particles.

faq.q: When is the Friedewald equation inaccurate?
faq.a: The Friedewald equation (LDL = Total − HDL − Trig/5) was derived in 1972 and assumes a fixed Trig:VLDL-cholesterol ratio of 5:1. It systematically underestimates LDL when triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL because the actual VLDL composition shifts. It also performs poorly at LDL <70 mg/dL — exactly the range where statin-treated high-risk patients live — leading to false reassurance. The Martin-Hopkins equation (JAMA 2013) uses an adjustable divisor matched to triglyceride and non-HDL strata and is accurate up to Trig ~800 mg/dL; it has been adopted as the default by Quest, LabCorp, and most major US health systems since 2018. For triglycerides above 400, a direct LDL assay (enzymatic or beta-quantification) is the standard. If your lab report shows 'LDL calc' with high triglycerides, ask your physician to order a direct LDL or repeat the panel after a 12-hour fast.

faq.q: ApoB vs LDL-C: which one should I track?
faq.a: Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) is a structural protein present in one copy per atherogenic particle (LDL, VLDL, IDL, Lp(a)). It is a direct count of atherogenic particles, whereas LDL-C measures the cholesterol mass carried in those particles. Sniderman et al. (JACC 2019) argued ApoB is causally upstream in atherosclerosis and a superior risk discriminator, particularly in patients with metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, or hypertriglyceridemia, where small dense LDL particles can produce 'normal' LDL-C readings but elevated particle number. The 2018 ACC/AHA guideline lists ApoB ≥130 mg/dL as a risk-enhancing factor, and the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (2021) and European Atherosclerosis Society now favor ApoB as a primary target. ApoB testing costs roughly the same as a basic lipid panel and is increasingly available. For most low-risk patients LDL-C remains sufficient; for discordance cases or metabolic syndrome, ApoB is worth adding.

faq.q: If my cholesterol is borderline, do I need a statin?
faq.a: Borderline cholesterol alone does not equal statin indication — the 2018 ACC/AHA framework decides therapy on overall ASCVD 10-year risk, not on isolated LDL values within the 70-189 range. Use the ASCVD Risk Estimator Plus (free at tools.acc.org/ascvd-risk-estimator-plus). For primary prevention adults 40-75 with LDL 70-189: risk <5% generally favors lifestyle alone; 5-7.5% (borderline risk) warrants a clinician-patient risk discussion and possibly coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring to refine the decision; 7.5-20% (intermediate risk) supports moderate-intensity statin after risk discussion; ≥20% (high risk) supports high-intensity statin without further stratification. Risk enhancers like family history of premature ASCVD, chronic inflammatory disease, LDL ≥160, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, persistently elevated triglycerides, elevated Lp(a), or elevated hs-CRP can shift a borderline case toward treatment.

faq.q: Triglycerides over 500 — is this an emergency?
faq.a: Triglycerides ≥500 mg/dL place you in the 'very high' category, and the immediate concern is acute pancreatitis, which becomes substantial at Trig >1000 mg/dL. If you have abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or signs of pancreatitis (epigastric pain radiating to the back, tender abdomen), go to the ER. Severe hypertriglyceridemia without symptoms warrants prompt evaluation, not necessarily ER triage. Treatment includes urgent dietary fat restriction (<15% of calories), strict alcohol avoidance, optimization of diabetes if present, and pharmacotherapy with fibrates (fenofibrate 145 mg/day), high-dose omega-3 (icosapent ethyl 2 g BID per REDUCE-IT), or niacin. Secondary causes to rule out: uncontrolled diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, estrogen therapy, beta-blockers, atypical antipsychotics, and excessive alcohol. Genetic causes (familial chylomicronemia, LPL deficiency) should be considered with Trig persistently >1000.

faq.q: Can a plant-based diet replace a statin?
faq.a: For patients with low to intermediate ASCVD risk and modest LDL elevation, a structured plant-based or Portfolio diet can produce LDL reductions of 13-30%, sometimes comparable to a low-intensity statin. The Portfolio Diet (Jenkins et al., JAMA 2003) combines plant sterols 2 g/day, soluble fiber 25-30 g/day from oats/barley/psyllium/legumes, soy protein, and tree nuts — average LDL reduction ~30% in compliant patients. The PREDIMED trial showed Mediterranean diet reduces major cardiovascular events by ~30% over 5 years. However, for patients with LDL ≥190 mg/dL, established ASCVD, familial hypercholesterolemia, or diabetes with 10-year risk ≥7.5%, lifestyle is adjunctive — not a substitute for statin therapy. The mortality benefit of statins in high-risk groups is established across dozens of randomized trials representing hundreds of thousands of patients (CTT meta-analyses, Lancet 2010 and 2012). Discontinuing or refusing statin therapy in high-risk patients in favor of diet alone is associated with worse outcomes.

faq.q: How often should I get a lipid panel?
faq.a: USPSTF and ACC/AHA recommend baseline lipid screening starting at age 20 for adults, with re-screening every 4-6 years if results are normal and risk is low. After age 40, more frequent screening (every 1-2 years) is reasonable given that the ASCVD risk calculator becomes more clinically actionable in that age range. Patients on statin therapy typically have a follow-up lipid panel 4-12 weeks after initiation or dose change to confirm response (target ≥30% LDL reduction with moderate intensity, ≥50% with high intensity), then every 3-12 months. Children with family history of premature ASCVD or FH should be screened starting at age 9-11 per AAP guidelines. Non-fasting lipid panels are acceptable for screening; fasting (12 hours) is preferred when triglycerides or calculated LDL are the focus.

faq.q: What is Lp(a) and should I be tested?
faq.a: Lipoprotein(a) — Lp(a) — is an LDL-like particle with apolipoprotein(a) covalently attached. Its concentration is ~90% genetically determined and changes little with lifestyle or statins. Elevated Lp(a) above 50 mg/dL (or 125 nmol/L) is an independent ASCVD risk factor present in approximately 20% of the global population. The 2018 ACC/AHA guideline lists Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL as a risk-enhancing factor. Current recommendation is to measure Lp(a) at least once in adulthood, especially in patients with personal or family history of premature ASCVD, recurrent events on optimal statin therapy, or familial hypercholesterolemia. There is no approved therapy that lowers Lp(a) meaningfully (niacin only modestly, PCSK9 inhibitors ~25%), but antisense oligonucleotide drugs (pelacarsen) targeting LPA mRNA are in phase 3 trials (HORIZON). Elevated Lp(a) generally argues for more aggressive LDL lowering with statins and ezetimibe.

faq.q: Are non-fasting lipid panels accurate enough?
faq.a: Yes, for most screening purposes. The 2016 European Atherosclerosis Society and European Federation of Clinical Chemistry consensus and the 2018 ACC/AHA guideline both endorse non-fasting lipid panels for routine cardiovascular risk assessment. Total cholesterol, HDL, and ApoB change minimally with eating. Triglycerides rise 10-20% postprandially; if non-fasting triglycerides are <175 mg/dL, the test is considered valid. Calculated LDL via Friedewald becomes unreliable when triglycerides are elevated, which is why Martin-Hopkins (which adjusts for postprandial state) has become the default calculation. A fasting panel is still preferred if triglycerides are being treated, if a calculated LDL is unexpectedly low, or if hypertriglyceridemia is suspected. Skipping the fast lowers patient burden and tends to improve screening adherence.

faq.q: Can I have normal cholesterol but still develop heart disease?
faq.a: Yes — roughly 50% of patients hospitalized with coronary heart disease have LDL cholesterol below 100 mg/dL. LDL is necessary but not sufficient: ASCVD risk also depends on Lp(a), ApoB particle number, inflammation (hs-CRP), endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, family history, sleep apnea, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, and psychosocial stress. Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring via non-contrast cardiac CT can detect subclinical atherosclerosis in patients with apparently normal lipids — a CAC score of 0 carries very low 10-year event risk regardless of other risk factors, while a CAC ≥100 or ≥75th percentile for age moves a patient toward statin therapy even with 'normal' LDL. The 2018 ACC/AHA guideline incorporates CAC scoring as a decision aid for borderline-risk and intermediate-risk patients (5-20% 10-year ASCVD risk).
